chunks: 171 - Al-Riḍā عليه السلام wrote to Muḥammad ibn Sinān regarding what he wrote in reply to his questions:

“The reason for the ghusl (ritual bath) of janābah is cleanliness: to purify the human being from what has affected him of harm, and to purify the rest of his body, because janābah comes forth from the whole body. Therefore, it is obligatory upon him to purify his whole body. And the reason for the easing in the case of urine and feces is that they are more frequent and more continuous than janābah, so concession was given in them with wudu (ablution) because of their frequency, their hardship, and their occurrence without intention from him and without desire. Janābah only occurs through enjoyment from themselves and compelling themselves.”

key_terms.النَّظَافَةُ: cleanliness as the stated rationale of the ruling
key_terms.الِاسْتِلْذَاذِ: enjoyment or pleasure associated with janabah
key_terms.الْبَوْلِ: urine, for which only wudu is required here
key_terms.الْغَائِطِ: feces, paired with urine in the ruling
key_terms.الْوُضُوءِ: ritual ablution deemed sufficient in the case mentioned
key_terms.تَطْهِيرِ الْإِنْسَانِ: purifying the person from what has affected him
key_terms.غُسْلِ الْجَنَابَةِ: the ritual bath required for the state of janabah

ai.seo_question: Why is ghusl obligatory for janabah but not for urine and feces in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith explains the legal wisdom behind ghusl for janabah and the lesser requirement of wudu for urine and feces. It states that janabah relates to the whole body and arises through pleasure, while urine and feces are more frequent and burdensome, so the law grants ease by requiring only wudu for them.
